issues.legal_issue: A preventive detention order is expressed to be made in the Governor’s name when its substance and wording show that it is made under the Governor’s authority, even if it does not use a prescribed formula.
material_facts: The order stated that the Government was satisfied and directed detention, and it concluded with the words “By order of the Governor.”
The High Court held that the order was defective because it did not expressly say it was made in the Governor’s name.
issues.conclusion: The order was expressed to be made in the Governor’s name and was not defective on that ground. The High Court’s order of release was wrong, although the State undertook not to re-arrest the detainee in respect of the matters in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Article 166(1) of the Constitution requires State executive action to be expressed in the Governor’s name, but substance rather than a magic formula controls. Section 3 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, authorises the State Government to make a detention order; section 3(43a)(a) of the General Clauses Act treats “State Government” in an enactment as the Governor. Because the order reproduced section 3’s language and concluded that it was by order of the Governor, it was in substance made in the Governor’s name.

rule.if: preventive_detention_order and states_government_is_satisfied and directs_persons_detention and concludes_by_order_of_governor

predicates.preventive_detention_order: The proceeding concerns an order directing a person’s preventive detention.
predicates.states_government_is_satisfied: The order states that the Government is satisfied that detention is necessary.
predicates.directs_persons_detention: The order directs that the person be detained.
predicates.concludes_by_order_of_governor: The order states that it is made by order of the Governor.

issues.definition: When a preventive detention order states the Government’s satisfaction, directs detention, and concludes that it is by order of the Governor, the order is expressed in the Governor’s name.

issues.legal_issue: A detention order that requires independent proof may be established by a believed affidavit from an official with the requisite means of knowledge; testimony from the Minister in charge is not invariably required.
material_facts: The High Court called for affidavits after considering that the detention order could not prove itself, and it was not satisfied with affidavits made by the Home Secretary.
The High Court considered that the Minister in charge should have made an affidavit.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether the affidavits in this case proved the order, because it held that the written order was not defective and the State did not seek re-arrest.
issues.conclusion: It is not necessary in every case to call the Minister in charge. If a Secretary or another person has the requisite means of knowledge and the affidavit is believed, that may be sufficient; the assessment depends on the facts of the case.
issues.legal_principle: The sufficiency and nature of evidence used to prove an executive order are matters of fact that may vary from case to case. A person’s state of mind may be proved by evidence other than that person’s own testimony. The Court left open the claim based on Article 163(3) of the Constitution.

rule.if: detention_challenge_proceeding and order_requires_independent_proof and official_has_requisite_means_of_knowledge and affidavit_is_believed

predicates.detention_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenges the validity of a detention order.
predicates.order_requires_independent_proof: The detention order cannot itself establish that it was validly made and must be proved by other evidence.
predicates.official_has_requisite_means_of_knowledg: An official other than the Minister has a sufficient basis for knowing whether the required decision was made.
predicates.affidavit_is_believed: The court accepts the official’s affidavit as credible.

issues.definition: In a challenge to detention, when an order requires independent proof, a credible affidavit from an official with the necessary knowledge can suffice without testimony from the Minister.

issues.legal_issue: An affidavit’s verification must distinguish matters based on personal knowledge from matters based on information and disclose the sources of information.
material_facts: The Home Secretary’s affidavit included matters known to him personally, but its verification stated generally that everything was true to the best of his information and belief.
The verification did not clearly identify the basis for the different matters or disclose sources of information for matters not based on personal knowledge.
issues.conclusion: The verification was defective. Verifications should follow the approach of Order XIX, rule 3, of the Code of Civil Procedure, whether or not that rule applies directly, and sources of information must be clearly disclosed when the statement is not based on personal knowledge.
issues.legal_principle: The Court endorsed the observations in Padmabati Dasi v. Rasik Lal Dhar and directed that affidavit verification be modelled on Order XIX, rule 3, of the Code of Civil Procedure, distinguishing personal knowledge from information and belief and disclosing the sources of information.

predicates.affidavit_in_detention_challenge: An affidavit is submitted in a proceeding challenging detention.
predicates.affidavit_contains_personal_and_informat: The affidavit includes some matters known personally and other matters not based on personal knowledge.
predicates.verification_uses_blanket_information_an: The verification applies a general statement of information and belief to all matters without distinguishing their basis.

issues.definition: When an affidavit in a detention challenge combines personal and informational matters but uses only a blanket verification based on information and belief, its verification is defective.

issues.legal_issue: Grounds furnished for preventive detention are sufficiently specific to support the Government’s satisfaction when they identify the alleged conduct and provide particulars about the people, area, and period involved.
material_facts: The grounds stated that the detainee was instigating people to commit violence against landlords in furtherance of a campaign against rent payment.
Further particulars identified tenants in specified villages and a district area and stated that the conduct had continued for some months until the arrest.
issues.conclusion: The grounds supplied were sufficiently specific and could form a proper basis for the Government’s satisfaction.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, the Government must be satisfied that detention is necessary for the specified preventive purpose. The Court held on the facts that the grounds supplied were sufficiently specific; it did not rely on an earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.preventive_detention_proceeding: The proceeding concerns detention ordered to prevent specified conduct.
predicates.grounds_identify_alleged_conduct: The furnished grounds describe the conduct said to justify detention.
predicates.grounds_identify_affected_people_area_an: The furnished grounds give particulars identifying the people or area involved and the period of the alleged conduct.

issues.definition: In a preventive detention proceeding, grounds describing the alleged conduct and providing particulars about the people, area, and period are sufficiently specific to support the Government’s satisfaction.
